issues.legal_issue: A respondent may challenge an adverse finding to support a decree in the respondent’s favour without filing cross-objections when seeking no additional relief.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the bank’s suit, leaving the decree in the borrower’s favour, although it rejected the borrower’s plea that the suit was barred by the rule against splitting claims.
The bank appealed, and the borrower relied on the rejected plea to resist the bank’s appeal.
The borrower sought to uphold the decree, not to obtain relief beyond it.
issues.conclusion: The borrower was entitled to challenge the trial court’s adverse finding without filing cross-objections.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XLI Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a respondent may support the decree by challenging a finding against them without cross-objections. Cross-objections are needed when the respondent seeks relief beyond what the decree has already granted.

predicates.appeal_from_favorable_decree: The opposing party appealed from a decree that was ultimately in the respondent’s favour.
predicates.respondent_challenges_adverse_finding: The respondent challenged a finding made against them by the lower court.
predicates.respondent_seeks_only_to_uphold_decree: The respondent sought to preserve the decree and did not seek additional relief.

issues.definition: When an appeal is brought against a decree in the respondent’s favour, the respondent may challenge an adverse finding without cross-objections if doing so only supports that decree.

issues.legal_issue: A later suit to enforce a mortgage is not barred merely because an earlier suit sought recovery of the loan debt without seeking mortgage relief.
material_facts: The bank first sued to recover the loan as a money claim and did not seek relief on the equitable mortgage in that suit.
After the bank could not recover the debt by proceeding against the hypothecated bus, it brought a separate suit to enforce the mortgage over immovable property.
The borrower did not produce the earlier plaint to establish that both suits rested on the same cause of action or that mortgage relief had been omitted without leave.
The later suit concerned enforcement of a mortgage by deposit of title deeds.
issues.conclusion: The later mortgage-enforcement suit was not barred by the rule against splitting claims.
issues.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 requires the plaintiff to include the whole claim arising from the cause of action sued upon; a bar requires proof that the later suit concerns the same cause of action, that further relief was available, and that it was omitted without leave. Under Order XXXIV Rules 14 and 15, a mortgagee seeking sale of mortgaged property must bring a suit for sale, and may do so notwithstanding Order II Rule 2. A plea under Order II Rule 2 based on an earlier suit must be proved by producing the earlier pleading: Gurbux Singh v. Bhooralal and M/s Bengal Waterproof Ltd. v. M/s Bombay Waterproof Manufacturing Co. The cause-of-action test is whether the new claim is founded on a cause of action distinct from the former one; different evidence supporting the claims indicates different causes of action: Payana Reena Saminatha v. Pana Lana Palaniappa and Mohammad Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Mian. The principles were reiterated in Sidramappa v. Rajashetty, Deva Ram v. Ishwar Chand, and State of Maharashtra v. National Construction Company.

rule.if: mortgage_enforcement_suit and prior_suit_sought_debt_recovery and prior_suit_omitted_mortgage_relief and defendant_did_not_produce_prior_pleading

predicates.mortgage_enforcement_suit: The plaintiff brought a suit seeking enforcement of a mortgage over property.
predicates.prior_suit_sought_debt_recovery: The plaintiff had earlier sued to recover the underlying debt as a money claim.
predicates.prior_suit_omitted_mortgage_relief: The earlier suit did not seek relief enforcing the mortgage.
predicates.defendant_did_not_produce_prior_pleading: The defendant relying on the earlier suit did not produce its pleading to establish the basis of the claim.

issues.definition: A later mortgage-enforcement suit is not barred when the earlier suit sought debt recovery without mortgage relief and the defendant does not produce the earlier pleading to establish the asserted bar.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court need not invoke its power to grant further relief when a plaintiff appeals the dismissal of the plaintiff’s suit and seeks the relief claimed at trial.
material_facts: The trial court dismissed the bank’s suit.
The bank appealed and sought the decree it had requested in its suit.
The High Court granted the bank a decree while purporting to rely on its power to grant further relief in an appeal.
issues.conclusion: There was no occasion to invoke the appellate power to grant further relief; the bank’s entitlement to the relief it sought was to be decided in its appeal on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers an appellate court to pass a decree that ought to have been passed, or grant further relief, including in appropriate circumstances in favour of a respondent who filed no appeal or objection. It need not be invoked where the plaintiff’s suit was dismissed and the plaintiff appeals seeking the relief claimed in the suit; the appellate court should decide the appeal and grant that relief if the plaintiff is entitled to it.

predicates.plaintiff_appeals_after_suit_dismissed: The plaintiff appealed after the trial court dismissed the plaintiff’s suit.
predicates.plaintiff_seeks_original_claimed_relief: The plaintiff sought on appeal the relief originally claimed in the suit.
predicates.appellate_court_decides_entitlement_on_m: The appellate court determines whether the plaintiff is entitled to the claimed relief by considering the merits of the appeal.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff appeals the dismissal of the suit to obtain the relief originally claimed, the appellate court decides entitlement on the merits without needing a separate power to grant further relief.

issues.legal_issue: A borrower’s liability is not discharged by an alleged transfer of the debt to another person unless a concluded arrangement taking over the liability is proved.
material_facts: The borrower claimed that a tripartite arrangement had transferred the bus and the loan liability to another person with the bank’s agreement.
The documents showed only an attempt to make such an arrangement and did not establish that it was concluded or that the bank agreed to the other person taking over the liability.
The borrower did not examine the alleged new debtor.
The bank’s payment of insurance premiums was consistent with its protection of the security and did not establish the alleged transfer.
issues.conclusion: The borrower did not prove a transfer of liability and remained liable for the debt.
issues.legal_principle: The party asserting that liability has ended by a transfer or novation bears the burden of proving the concluded arrangement and the creditor’s agreement to the substitution. Evidence showing only an attempted arrangement does not establish novation or discharge.

rule.if: appeal_from_debt_liability_decree and borrower_asserts_liability_transfer and evidence_shows_only_attempted_arrangement and alleged_new_debtor_not_examined

predicates.appeal_from_debt_liability_decree: A borrower appealed a decree holding the borrower liable for a debt.
predicates.borrower_asserts_liability_transfer: The borrower claimed that another person had taken over the debt with the creditor’s agreement.
predicates.evidence_shows_only_attempted_arrangemen: The evidence established only an attempt to arrange a transfer, not a concluded agreement accepted by the creditor.
predicates.alleged_new_debtor_not_examined: The borrower did not call the alleged new debtor to give evidence supporting the transfer.

issues.definition: A borrower remains liable when the borrower asserts a transfer of the debt but the evidence shows only an attempted arrangement and the alleged new debtor is not examined.
